title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
1. Setup
Start n4.R with these lines. Every lesson script from now on starts the same way.

library(tidyverse)
library(srvyr)

analysis <- readRDS("data/nhis_analysis.rds")

If readRDS() says the file does not exist, run prepare.R first (N3, section 6).

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
2. What a weight is
Each adult in the file has a weight, WTFA_A: the number of U.S. adults that person stands for.

summary(analysis$WTFA_A)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   2358    5835    9020   10936   13371   45481 


The median person stands for about 9,000 adults, but weights range from about 2,400 to 45,000. Someone with a weight of 45,000 belongs to a group that was hard to reach or less likely to respond, so each person interviewed from that group has to stand for many more people. Someone with a small weight belongs to a group that was easy to reach.






NoteYour turn 1



Add up all the weights with sum(). What does the total represent?
Expected result: 264,821,349, about 265 million: the number of U.S. adults the survey represents (adults living in households, not in institutions such as nursing homes or prisons).








TipSolution






sum(analysis$WTFA_A)

[1] 264821349

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
3. Unweighted versus weighted
How many U.S. adults are 65 or older? Here is the share of the sample, and the share once each person counts as many people as their weight says. weighted.mean() does that.

analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(age_group)) %>%
  summarize(
    unweighted = 100 * mean(age_group == "65+"),
    weighted   = 100 * weighted.mean(age_group == "65+", WTFA_A)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  unweighted weighted
       <dbl>    <dbl>
1      35.06    23.26


More than a third of the people interviewed are 65 or older, but they make up less than a quarter of U.S. adults. Older adults are more likely to live alone or with just one other adult (and only one adult per household is interviewed), and they are more likely to take part, so the sample has too many of them. Each of them gets a smaller weight to make up for it.
This matters for the project because cancer is much more common at older ages. Any unweighted estimate about survivors leans toward older people.






NoteYour turn 2



What percent of U.S. adults are cancer survivors? Calculate it unweighted and weighted, leaving out people with missing survivor.
Expected result: 11.7% unweighted, 8.7% weighted.








TipSolution






analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(survivor)) %>%
  summarize(
    unweighted = 100 * mean(survivor),
    weighted   = 100 * weighted.mean(survivor, WTFA_A)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  unweighted weighted
       <dbl>    <dbl>
1      11.72    8.703

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
4. Why weights are not enough
weighted.mean() gives the right estimate. It cannot tell you how certain that estimate is, and every estimate from a sample needs a measure of uncertainty, usually a 95% confidence interval.
Uncertainty depends on how the sample was drawn, and the NHIS was not drawn one person at a time:

Clusters (sampling units). The NHIS first picks geographic areas, then households within them. People in the same area tend to be alike, so 30 people from one area tell you less than 30 people from 30 different areas. The column PPSU records each person’s primary sampling unit (PSU).
Strata. The country is first divided into groups of areas called strata, and areas are picked within each one. This makes estimates more precise. The column PSTRAT records the stratum.

Software that ignores clusters treats everyone as independent, and its confidence intervals come out too narrow: they claim more certainty than the data support.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
5. The survey design object
The srvyr package stores the data together with the design in one object. Everything after this works on that object instead of on analysis.

nhis_design <- analysis %>%
  as_survey_design(
    ids = PPSU,          # primary sampling units (clusters)
    strata = PSTRAT,     # strata
    weights = WTFA_A,    # weights
    nest = TRUE          # PSU numbers restart within each stratum
  )

nhis_design

Stratified 1 - level Cluster Sampling design (with replacement)
With (608) clusters.
Called via srvyr
Sampling variables:
  - ids: PPSU 
  - strata: PSTRAT 
  - weights: WTFA_A 
Data variables: 
  - HHX (chr), WTFA_A (dbl), PSTRAT (dbl), PPSU (dbl), fair_poor (dbl),
    survivor (dbl), poverty (fct), education (fct), age (dbl), age_group (chr),
    sex (chr), insured (chr)


Each argument names a column from the file. These four lines come straight from NCHS’s own instructions for analyzing the NHIS in R, in the 2025 survey description.






NoteWhy nest = TRUE?



PSU numbers are only unique within a stratum: two different areas in two different strata can share a number.

n_distinct(analysis$PPSU)                     # PSU numbers

[1] 606

nrow(distinct(analysis, PSTRAT, PPSU))        # actual PSUs

[1] 608


nest = TRUE tells R to identify a PSU by its stratum and its number. Without it, R would merge areas that are really separate.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
6. Estimates with confidence intervals
Use summarize() on the design object, with survey_mean() in place of mean(). vartype = "ci" asks for a 95% confidence interval, and na.rm = TRUE leaves out missing values.

nhis_design %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci"))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
      <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1    0.1472        0.1409        0.1534


survey_mean() gives a proportion. About 14.7% of U.S. adults report fair or poor health, and the 95% confidence interval runs from 14.1% to 15.3%. (The unweighted figure would have been 15.8%.)
group_by() works on the design just as it does on a dataframe.






NoteYour turn 3



Estimate the percent in fair or poor health for survivors and non-survivors, with 95% confidence intervals. Start from nhis_design, remove missing survivor with filter(), then use group_by() and survey_mean(). Multiply by 100 with mutate() if you like.
Expected result: survivors 27.4% (95% CI 25.3% to 29.5%); non-survivors 13.5% (12.9% to 14.1%).








TipSolution






nhis_design %>%
  filter(!is.na(survivor)) %>%
  group_by(survivor) %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci")) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("fair_poor"), ~ 100 * .x))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  survivor fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
     <dbl>     <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1        0     13.50         12.87         14.14
2        1     27.42         25.34         29.51


across(starts_with("fair_poor"), ~ 100 * .x) multiplies every column whose name starts with fair_poor (the estimate and both limits) by 100.



Among survivors, the weighted estimate (27.4%) is close to the unweighted one from N2 (26.9%). Weighting does not always change an estimate much, as here, but sometimes it does, as with age. You only know by doing it.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
7. Seeing what the design does
Here is the same estimate, fair or poor health among survivors, calculated three ways.

# 1. Ignoring the design: a simple confidence interval for a proportion
surv <- analysis %>% filter(survivor == 1, !is.na(fair_poor))
p <- mean(surv$fair_poor)
se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nrow(surv))
c(estimate = p, low = p - 1.96 * se, high = p + 1.96 * se) * 100

estimate      low     high 
26.88096 25.24782 28.51410 

# 2. Weights only
analysis %>%
  as_survey_design(weights = WTFA_A) %>%
  filter(survivor == 1) %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci") * 100)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
      <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1     27.42         25.45         29.39

# 3. The full design
nhis_design %>%
  filter(survivor == 1) %>%
  summarize(fair_poor = survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci") * 100)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  fair_poor fair_poor_low fair_poor_upp
      <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1     27.42         25.34         29.51





Method
Estimate
95% CI
Width




Ignoring the design
26.9%
25.2 to 28.5
3.3


Weights only
27.4%
25.5 to 29.4
3.9


Full design
27.4%
25.3 to 29.5
4.2




The weights fix the estimate (26.9% becomes 27.4%).
The strata and PSUs fix the uncertainty: the honest interval is about a quarter wider than the naive one.

The difference here is modest. For smaller groups and for variables that cluster strongly by place, such as income, it can be much larger. Since you cannot know in advance, always use the full design.

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
8. From percentages to people
Weights also turn counts of people in the sample into counts of people in the country. survey_total() adds up the weights.






NoteYour turn 4



How many U.S. adults are cancer survivors? Use group_by(survivor) and survey_total(vartype = "ci") on nhis_design. Dividing by 1e6 (one million) makes the numbers easier to read.
Expected result: about 23.0 million survivors (95% CI 21.8 to 24.2 million). The other rows are non-survivors and people with missing survivor.








TipSolution






nhis_design %>%
  group_by(survivor) %>%
  summarize(adults = survey_total(vartype = "ci")) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("adults"), ~ .x / 1e6))   # in millions

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  survivor   adults adults_low adults_upp
     <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1        0 241.5      233.8      249.2   
2        1  23.02      21.83      24.22  
3       NA   0.2731     0.1688     0.3774


2,833 people in the sample stand for about 23 million U.S. adults. (Remember the definition from N2: non-melanoma skin cancer alone does not count.)

title: N4 · Why Weights Matter
text:
Recap







Code
What it does




weighted.mean(x, w)
Weighted mean or proportion, without uncertainty


as_survey_design(ids = PPSU, strata = PSTRAT, weights = WTFA_A, nest = TRUE)
The NHIS design object


survey_mean(x, na.rm = TRUE, vartype = "ci")
Weighted mean or proportion with a 95% CI


survey_total(vartype = "ci")
Estimated number of people, with a 95% CI


group_by() on the design
Estimates for each group



The rule: weights for the estimate; strata and PSUs for the uncertainty; always all three.

title: R for Survey Data
text:
National surveys like the NHIS do not sample people at random from the whole population. To describe the population correctly, every analysis must account for the survey’s weights and design. These lessons teach that, using the 2025 NHIS Sample Adult file.
Running example: among adults who have had cancer, how does self-rated health differ by socioeconomic position?

title: Tutorials
text: Hands-on tutorials to introduce basic programming skills to conduct computational health research. No programming experience is needed: everyone starts with R Foundations, then continues with the tutorial that matches their project.

title: Tutorials
text:
How the tutorials work

Start in your browser. Early lessons are Google Colab notebooks: click a link, sign in with a Google account, and run code with nothing to install.
Move to RStudio for projects. Later lessons are run in RStudio on your own computer, where your files and packages stay put.
Learn by doing. Every lesson has exercises with expected results, and solutions at the end.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
In this lesson you will learn to:
Before this lesson: N2: Preparing Variables.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
1. Why move?
Colab was a good place to start: nothing to install. For a real project it has three problems:

Everything disappears when the session ends: your data, your files, and every package you installed.
Packages must be reinstalled every session. The survey packages used from N4 on take a while to install.
Real projects have many files (data, scripts, results) that need to stay together.

RStudio runs on your own computer. You install things once, and your files stay where you put them. From here on, you will read each lesson on this website and type the code into RStudio.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
2. Install R and RStudio
You need two programs, installed in this order:

R, the language itself: download it from CRAN. Choose your operating system (for a Mac, choose the version that matches your processor: Apple silicon or Intel) and install it with the default settings.
RStudio Desktop, the program you work in: download it from Posit and install it.

You only ever open RStudio. It finds R by itself.






TipA university computer?



If you cannot install software on your computer, ask your instructor about Posit Cloud, which runs RStudio in a web browser.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
3. Get the starter project
An RStudio project is a folder that holds everything for one piece of work, plus a small .Rproj file. Opening the .Rproj file opens RStudio inside that folder, so file paths like data/nhis2025_adult.csv just work.

Download nhis-project.zip (about 1.3 MB).
Unzip it and move the nhis-project folder somewhere permanent, such as your Documents folder.

On Windows, right-click the zip file and choose Extract All. Do not work inside the zip file itself; it only looks like a folder.
On a Mac, double-click the zip file.

Double-click nhis-project.Rproj to open the project in RStudio.

The folder contains:



File
What it is




nhis-project.Rproj
Opens the project


data/nhis2025_adult.csv
The NHIS teaching file from N1 and N2


prepare.R
The N2 code, as a script


n3.R … n7.R
Empty scripts, one for each lesson

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
4. A tour of RStudio
RStudio has four panes:








Pane
Where
What it is for




Source
top left
Scripts: code you write and save. Open n3.R to see it.


Console
bottom left
Where code actually runs, and where results appear


Environment
top right
The objects you have created, such as dataframes


Files
bottom right
The files in your project folder



A script is just a text file of R code. Unlike a Colab notebook, the results are not saved in the file; they appear in the Console when you run the code.
Two ways to run code from a script:

Run the current line (or selected lines): Ctrl + Enter on Windows, Cmd + Enter on a Mac.
Run the whole script from top to bottom: the Source button at the top of the script, or Ctrl + Shift + S / Cmd + Shift + S.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
5. Install the packages
Packages are installed once per computer, then loaded with library() in every script. Type this into the Console (not a script, since you never need to run it again) and press Enter:

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "survey", "srvyr"))

This can take several minutes. When it finishes, check that each one loads:

library(tidyverse)
library(survey)
library(srvyr)

Messages are normal; an error that says there is no package called ... means the installation did not finish. These lessons were tested with tidyverse 2.0.0, survey 4.5, and srvyr 1.3.1. You can check yours with packageVersion("srvyr").

survey is the standard R package for analyzing complex survey data.
srvyr lets you use survey methods with the same %>%, filter(), group_by(), and summarize() you already know. You will use it from N4 on.

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
6. Run the preparation script
Open prepare.R from the Files pane. It is the code you wrote in N2, as one script. Read through it: every step should look familiar. Then click Source to run it all.
It reads the teaching file, builds the analysis variables, and saves the result as data/nhis_analysis.rds.






NoteWhy .rds and not .csv?



A CSV file holds only text and numbers. An .rds file saves an R object exactly as it is, including details such as the order of the categories you set with factor() in N2. Use saveRDS() to save and readRDS() to read.


analysis now appears in the Environment pane: 24,215 observations of 12 variables.






NoteYour turn 1



In the Console, check the analysis file with dim(analysis) and count(analysis, survivor).
Expected result: 24,215 rows and 12 columns; 2,833 survivors, 21,349 non-survivors, 33 NA.








TipSolution






dim(analysis)

[1] 24215    12

count(analysis, survivor)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  survivor     n
     <dbl> <int>
1        0 21349
2        1  2833
3       NA    33

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
7. Your first script
Now write code in n3.R, where it is saved. A script should be able to run on its own from a fresh start, so it begins by loading its packages and its data.






NoteYour turn 2



In n3.R, write a script that:

loads the tidyverse,
reads data/nhis_analysis.rds with readRDS(),
calculates, for survivors only, the percent in fair or poor health in each poverty group, as you did for education in N2.

Save the script (Ctrl + S / Cmd + S), then run it with Source.
Expected result: Below 100% 57.8%; 100-199% 40.8%; 200-399% 27.5%; 400% or more 15.7%.








TipSolution






library(tidyverse)

analysis <- readRDS("data/nhis_analysis.rds")


analysis %>%
  filter(survivor == 1, !is.na(fair_poor)) %>%
  group_by(poverty) %>%
  summarize(people = n(), pct_fair_poor = 100 * mean(fair_poor))

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  poverty      people pct_fair_poor
  <fct>         <int>         <dbl>
1 Below 100%      206          57.8
2 100-199%        495          40.8
3 200-399%        891          27.5
4 400% or more   1239          15.7

title: N3 · Moving to RStudio
text:
8. The fresh-start test
A script that works only because of something you typed earlier in the Console will fail for anyone else, including you next week. Test it the way a stranger would run it:

Session > Restart R. This clears everything from memory; the Environment pane empties.
Run n3.R with Source.

If it still gives the same result, the script is complete. If you get an error such as object 'analysis' not found, something the script needs is missing from it.






NoteYour turn 3



Do the fresh-start test on n3.R.
Expected result: the same four percentages as before, with no errors.








TipSolution





If it failed, the most likely cause is a missing library(tidyverse) or readRDS() line at the top of the script. Every lesson script from now on starts with those two lines (plus library(srvyr) from N4).

text:
Recap







Step
How




Open the project
Double-click nhis-project.Rproj


Install a package (once per computer)
install.packages("name") in the Console


Load a package (every script)
library(name) at the top of the script


Run a line / the whole script
Ctrl/Cmd + Enter / Source


Save and read an R object
saveRDS(x, "file.rds"), readRDS("file.rds")


Check a script is complete
Session > Restart R, then Source
